newsitem.title: USA: Get the right credit card for the season.
newsitem.headline: Get the right credit card for the season.

text.p: When the days shorten and the temperatures drop, the credit card market gets hot enough to melt plastic.

Credit card issuers introduce new cards in the hopes of capturing borrowers for the hectic holiday season, according to Robert McKinley, president of CardTrak, a Frederick, Maryland, company which tracks the card industry.
Consumers are happy to oblige: Americans can be expected to pile almost $2.8 million a minute on their credit cards buying toys, gifts, food and clothes for the holidays.

This year, consumers should shop for cards before they shop for cranberries. With issuers getting increasingly sophisticated about targeting their cards' features for the most desireable customers, the market is more confusing than ever. With shoppers' own use patterns as varied as the sweaters and ties they'll buy, there are no simplistic "best cards for everyone."
To find the best card for you, first analyse your use pattern. The two basics are "revolvers," who always carry balances, and "convenience users" who always pay off their charges every month.

Within those categories there are many gradations. Some revolvers pay only minimums, a horrible habit that can leave them with 30 years of payments on a $2,000 debt. Other revolvers pay bigger chunks, but keep piling on more charges so they hardly ever get in the clear.
Some convenience users only use their cards for emergencies, or special large purchases, or travel expenses.

Others are disciplined enough to buy every carton of eggs and loaf of bread on their credit cards and then pay them off. Then there are the convenience users who slip a couple times a year and carry balances -- just for one month.
Be honest about your own use, because the wrong kind of card can really cost you. Once you've identified yourself, look for a card that has the best features for your use patterns.
If you're a little schizophrenic in your credit habits, consider getting a couple of cards to reflect your different borrowing habits.
If you're a revolver who only pays minimums, get a card that forces you to pay a higher minimum, or at least rewards you for doing so. McKinley touts Cleveland-based KeyBank's new "Key Smart" card.
This one drops your interest rate if you'll make higher minimum payments, and agree to an annual fee.

A KeySmart Gold card with no annual fee and a 2 percent minimum payment will charge interest at an annual rate of 17.9 percent interest. Agree to a $30 annual fee and a monthly payment that is 5 percent of your outstanding balance, and the rate drops all the way to 8.9 percent a year.
What's the difference? Several thousand dollars and about 23 years, according to calculations on credit card software from The Banker's Secret in Elmira, New York.

If you paid minimums only on the low-minimum, high interest rate card, it would take you 30 years and $6,827 to burn $2,000. The high-minimum low rate card would wipe out the same debt in a little more than six years and cost $2,513, even counting the annual fees.
If you're a revolver who pays off big chunks, you don't have to worry about forcing yourself into higher minimum payments, just go for the card with the lowest interest rate.

McKinley says right now the bank offering the lowest permanent (not introductory) rate is Huntington National Bank in Ohio, where a $50 annual fee buys you an 8.25 percent interest rate. Is it worth it? Probably, if you are carrying at least a $1,700 balance. The annual fee is worth about 3 percent a year off of that amount.
If you're a convenience user who doesn't use your card much, or one who occasionally lapses into revolver status, go for a no-fee card with the lowest rate possible.

This month, that's the AFBA Industrial Bank in Colorado, which offers no fees and 11.4 percent interest. And a special warning to the occasional lapsers out there; you know who you are. You're especially hurt by the practice of some issuers of assessing interest on a two-month average balance calculating period, says the Bankcard Holders of America. Slip one month and you can end up paying interest on extra charges you pay off immediately.

Finally, if you are one of the most disciplined of the convenience users, make hay while the sun shines. Find a good rebate card that pays you back and doesn't collect an annual fee, but don't be too surprised if it doesn't last.
Last month, GE fired the first shot when it told convenience users it was going to charge them to keep the card, but other lenders may follow suit.

In the meantime consider cars like the Chase Manhattan Cash Builder or the Discover Card. Or be realistic about your monthly charging activity and decide an annual fee is worth it. Or look local: Many grocery chains are offering their own co-branded cards that can net you as much as 3 percent off of your grocery bill and 1 percent off of everything else you buy.
